summary: Reviews the existing ways of renumbering a site, meaning changing its network addresses, for both IPv4 and IPv6, and points out operational problems with them. It also summarises proposals for new mechanisms and ends with a gap analysis of where more work is needed. It is informational, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Network renumbering means changing the IP prefixes used by a site. This RFC explains why existing tools do not update every address reference automatically and identifies work that could make renumbering easier.

subtitle: Why changing a site's IP prefixes remains an operational challenge

tldr.problem: A site may need new network prefixes after a provider change, network reorganization or merger. Addresses are stored in applications, devices, DNS and configuration, so a change can leave stale references behind.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews DHCP, IPv6 autoconfiguration, router advertisements, DNS and service discovery, then describes operational issues, proposals and remaining gaps.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational survey rather than a renumbering procedure. It recommends planning for IPv6 renumbering from the start of deployment.

facts.label: Address transition mechanism
facts.value: DHCP, SLAAC and overlapping IPv6 prefixes

today: RFC 5887 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It reviews renumbering mechanisms and operational gaps rather than specifying a procedure.

sections.title: When a Site Needs New Addresses
sections.content:
A medium or large site may need to renumber when it changes or adds a service provider, when its provider changes its own addresses, when the site reorganizes its subnets, or when networks merge or split. The RFC revisits a problem identified earlier and says that, despite available mechanisms, site renumbering is still viewed as expensive and error-prone.

The document focuses on planned or unplanned changes at medium and large sites, not routine address changes for small client devices or roaming users. It notes that sites may avoid renumbering by using private addresses and NAT, but that choice can constrain other network approaches. IP address lifetimes are generally not visible to applications after addresses reach the socket interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A site may need new addresses after a provider change, a network reorganization or a merger. Changing prefixes is difficult because software and configuration may keep using the old addresses.

sections.title: Existing Address and Router Mechanisms
sections.content:
DHCP can assign host addresses and related network parameters. IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration uses router advertisements that can announce more than one prefix and mark an old prefix as deprecated. DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation can provide prefixes to routers, while the IPv6 model allows multiple addresses and prefixes to overlap during a transition.

DNS records must also be updated when hosts change addresses. Secure Dynamic DNS Update can let a host report a new address, and service-discovery systems can reduce the need to store service addresses in advance. These mechanisms help with parts of renumbering, but do not automatically update every application or device configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP and IPv6 router advertisements can provide new addresses, while DNS updates can publish them. These tools help, but applications and other systems may still hold old addresses.

sections.title: What Breaks During Renumbering
sections.content:
TCP connections and UDP flows use source and destination IP addresses, so they generally do not survive an address change at either endpoint. Applications may cache addresses or put literal addresses in URLs, cookies or proxy settings. DNS pinning can also make some browsers keep using an earlier address despite a DNS change.

Routers may cache addresses, tunnels and VPNs may contain fixed endpoints, and routing rules, firewall rules, access lists and management databases may need updates. DNS forward and reverse records must be coordinated. IPv6 can overlap old and new prefixes during a planned transition, but tools and operating procedures must handle both prefixes during that period.
sections.plainLanguage: A change can disrupt active connections and leave stale addresses in programs, routers, VPNs, firewalls and DNS. IPv6 can use old and new prefixes for a time, but the site's tools must manage that overlap.

sections.title: Security Risks of Address Changes
sections.content:
Automatic prefix announcements need protection against spoofing, because an attacker who changes a site's addresses could divert traffic or disrupt service. Firewall and access-control rules should be updated in two stages: install rules for new addresses before the change, then remove old rules after it. Leaving old rules in place can allow access that should no longer be permitted.

Certificates that contain an IP address can become invalid when that address changes; the RFC recommends DNS names instead for the certificate subject alternative name. It also notes that DNS security and authenticated updates are important when DNS communicates new addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Fake address-change information could redirect or interrupt traffic. Security rules need to cover the new addresses before the change and remove the old addresses afterward.

sections.title: Proposals and Remaining Gaps
sections.content:
The RFC surveys proposals such as SHIM6, Mobile IP, HIP and SCTP that can separate a connection's identity from the address used to forward packets. It also mentions configuration and autoconfiguration work. These are approaches under discussion in the document, not a single solution adopted by this RFC.

The gap analysis calls for applications to learn address lifetimes, better name-based APIs, router and address-management tools that handle multiple prefixes, secure DNS updates, and operational guidance. It recommends that IPv6 network plans make provision for future renumbering.
sections.plainLanguage: Some proposals aim to keep a connection working while its network address changes. The RFC also calls for better software, management tools and operating procedures, and recommends planning for renumbering from the start.
